The document titled The Global Practice of After Action Review: A Systematic Review of Literature was prepared by Landry Ndri Ko Mayigane, Nicolas Isla, Emanuele Bruni, Frederik Copper, and Stella Chungong. It acknowledges contributions from various experts and organizations, including the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Lund University, the World Food Programme, and Tohoku University, among others. An After Action Review (AAR) is a qualitative evaluation of actions taken during an emergency response. Its purpose is to identify best practices, gaps, and lessons learned to improve future preparedness and response systems. AARs are not external evaluations of individual or team performance but rather constructive, collective learning opportunities. They aim to foster open and honest discussions among stakeholders to identify what worked, what did not, and how improvements can be made. AARs can range from informal debriefings to structured workshops with multisectoral participation. The WHO recommends that Member States conduct AARs as part of the International Health Regulations (IHR) Monitoring and Evaluation Framework (MEF). This framework assesses the functionality of core capacities and contributes to the development of comprehensive national action plans for health security. AARs are particularly valuable for identifying strengths, weaknesses, and actionable recommendations to enhance emergency response capabilities. The literature review conducted for this document examined 122 sources, including methodological reports and AAR case studies. It highlighted the importance of systematic post-event learning to build a culture of continuous improvement. AARs are relatively quick and cost-effective to conduct, relying on open and equal interaction among participants. They follow a consistent analytical structure, addressing key questions such as what should have happened, what actually occurred, what went well or poorly, and how improvements can be made. AARs are versatile tools applicable to various events, including emergencies, disasters, and public health crises. They provide a platform for analyzing successes and failures, identifying root causes, and developing strategies to address them. By capturing lessons learned and best practices, AARs contribute to institutional memory and inform decision-making for future events. The WHO has developed guidance and toolkits to standardize and simplify the AAR process, including templates, checklists, and facilitator manuals. The findings of this review emphasize the critical role of AARs in fostering organizational learning and improving emergency preparedness and response. They serve as a mechanism for translating experiences into actionable plans and recommendations, which can be integrated into national planning cycles. The WHO's guidance and tools aim to support Member States in conducting effective AARs and building a global repository of lessons learned to enhance health security worldwide.
